https://www.irishmirror.ie/government-je.text: The government jet took off for Dubai this morning as the operation to bring Daniel Kinahan back to Ireland finally got underway. The Irish Air Corps €53 million Dassault Falcon 6X took off at 10.30am on Saturday morning and will land in the United Arab Emirates city in the evening. Mob boss Kinahan (49) is then expected to be flown back to Ireland on the jet and will land at the Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnell, Dublin on Sunday afternoon. Gardaí are on board the direct flight to the United Arab Emirates as part of a complex operation that has been meticulously planned for several weeks. The handover will then occur as Dubai Police oversee Kinahan’s extradition from the Middle-Eastern sanctuary he has called home for the past decade. Officers are also prepared for potential delays - and sources stressed that the operation's exact timing could change at any time. This is the first time the government jet, which was purchased last year, will be used to transport an alleged criminal to this country. The jet, which has a call sign of ‘Irl290,’ is typically used to ferry the Taoiseach and government ministers around the globe. It has however also been used to transport members of the Ranger Wing to and from locations, as well as to pick up people in emergency situations. In past similar operations an Irish Air Corps Airbus C295 was used to pick up Gerry ‘The Monk’ Hutch and Sean McGovern. However, the government jet is far more efficient because it can quickly make the journey from Dubai without any stops. A source said: “This is ultimately about getting Kinahan to Ireland as quickly and as securely as possible - both for him and the gardaí with him.” This weekend’s security operation is set to involve the Defence Forces , Irish Prison Service and multiple Garda units, including the Armed Support Unit, Emergency Response Unit, National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau, and Garda Air Support. Gardaí and the Defence Forces have declined to comment on the operation when contacted last night. Several road closures are also expected as gardaí are hopeful of moving Kinahan straight to the Special Criminal Court without delay. Once back on Irish soil Kinahan will be arrested on the tarmac in relation to directing a criminal organisation. He can be charged once he enters the confines of the court. It is understood the charge encompasses a number of murder plots carried out over the course of the Kinahan Hutch feud - which first erupted in September 2015. While the exact details of the security operation are being kept under wraps, sources say Kinahan will be immediately brought from Baldonnell to Dublin’s Criminal Courts of Justice in Parkgate Street under a heavy armed escort. As with his right-hand man Sean McGovern, Kinahan may be driven out of the military airport in an unmarked Garda car, while ‘decoy’ vehicles could also be used. If this approach occurs, it will be followed in the front and back by several other unmarked vehicles carrying armed gardaí. However sources say it is also possible that another extraordinary step could be taken in light of the security concerns surrounding the operation. Sources say Kinahan could potentially be flown out of Baldonnel via helicopter to another location, where he may then be more speedily transported to the Special Criminal Court. It is understood special arrangements have been made to open the doors of the courts in Parkgate Street for a hearing on Sunday. Three judges of the Special Criminal Court will be in place as Kinahan is escorted under armed guard from the basement of the building, where he will have been driven in just moments before. The court will then hear evidence of Kinahan’s arrest, charge and caution from a senior Garda. Kinahan is entitled to legal representation and to be present in court for the brief hearing. It is then expected that he will be remanded into custody, and gardaí will hand him over to the Irish Prison Service. Kinahan will likely be brought back down into the basement of the courts building, where he will enter a newly purchased prison van. The Irish Prison Service recently purchased the bullet-and-bomb-proof van from the UK to carry the likes of Kinahan and other high profile prisoners in the future. Gardaí will escort the van to Portlaoise Prison in Co Laois, the country’s maximum security prison. Documents will then be signed to transfer Kinahan to the prison as a remand prisoner. He will then be housed on the ‘A’ Block of the prison, which is deemed to be the most secure section. The ‘A’ is also home to Sean McGovern, who was recently jailed for 24 years for his role in directing a criminal organisation in relation to the murder of innocent Dad Noel ‘Duck Egg’ Kirwan and in relation to the surveillance and targeting of Hutch associate James ‘Mago’ Gately. Sources say Kinahan is however likely to be held in isolation for the duration of his remand. It is also envisaged that his future court hearings before a trial would be held via video link. A trial is not expected to take place until at least a year from now - with sources previously stating that the file in the case is extremely large. Prison authorities have also stepped up security measures in Portlaoise - with Kinahan likely to be kept on ‘suicide watch’ for a period of time. The case against Daniel Kinahan is understood to allege that he directed the Kinahan organisation during the course of the murderous feud that saw 18 people killed. It is understood to specifically allege that Kinahan directed the criminal gang in the attempt to murder Hutch associate ‘Mago’ from October 2015 into mid 2017. It is also understood to relate to a plot to murder ‘The Monk’ himself in Lanzarote in December 2015. Some of the allegations against Kinahan are believed to rely on encrypted conversations uncovered from the seizure of several phones from the cartel. The so-called ‘Pretty Good Privacy’ (PGP) devices contain conversations between someone who will be alleged to be Kinahan - and Sean McGovern - as well as other associates. McGovern, who was Kinahan’s closest confidant, was nailed in part by encrypted conversations intercepted by gardaí that showed how he and other cartel members plotted the murder of Mr Kirwan and set about targeting Gately. Gardaí are understood to allege that encrypted handles known as ‘Bon Neww,’ 'Bon4' and 'Cap' which communicated with and gave orders to McGovern and others at the height of the feud, belonged to Daniel Kinahan. In one conversation revealed during McGovern’s case, the Special Criminal Court heard how Sean McGovern told 'Cap' following the Regency Hotel shooting : “Mate I’m fuming I swear to God what about doing Mink’s daughter or will that bring too much heat?” ‘Cap’ then responded, “Yes, but maybe only Neddie,” in a message referencing Eddie Hutch, a brother of Gerry ‘The Monk’ Hutch. Those messages were sent on February 7th, 2017, just one day before Eddie was ultimately murdered by the cartel at his home in Poplar Row in Dublin. Other encrypted chats revealed that the cartel plot to track James Gately was first hatched in October 2015 and later in 2017 ‘Bon Neww’ directed McGovern to go after him. “Hate the horrible rat bag. Get Mago,” Bon Neww (allegedly Kinahan) told McGovern in April 2017. On April 3rd, 2017, Estonian hitman Imre Arakas flew into Ireland and the following day was arrested by gardaí at an address at Blakestown Cottages. Officers ultimately seized a Blackberry device containing the encrypted instructions he was receiving from the handle they suspect was Kinahan. The court heard how a member of the Garda Emergency Response Unit took photos of the conversations before they were remotely wiped. In those messages Arakas was conversing with ‘Bon Neww’ about using a ‘silencer’ and shooting Gately in the head from a distance. The court also heard that ‘Bon Neww’ relayed messages to Arakas, including informing him that Gately ‘drives most days, he seems to go to Newry and back.’ Arakas was also told to Google a picture of Gately, with the message informing him that the second image on the site was a clear picture of him. https://oilprice.com/Geopolitics/Europe/.text: US President Donald Trump told reporters that he does not believe Moscow will attack a NATO nation amid rising concerns that Russian President Vladimir Putin will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test the Western alliance's resolve. Trump on August 27 told reporters in the Oval Office that he had engaged in "good talks" with Putin and that "he's not going to be attacking a NATO territory." He did not specify when those talks were held. "I am not concerned...at all. There is no problem," Trump was quoted earlier as saying by news publication Axios when asked about a possible Russian provocation against a NATO state. The remarks come as the Kremlin, at the same time, dismissed as "scare stories" reports in the US media suggesting Moscow could attack NATO and following a surprise visit by the CIA director to Moscow. NATO Article 5 Assurances Western European security has long been tied to NATO's mutual defense clause, Article 5, which states that an attack on one member nation constitutes an attack on all. Many Western leaders and officials have expressed concerns over Trump's commitment to the military alliance. Trump has at times put into question a possible US response to an attack on a member state, while at other times reaffirming support for NATO. A letter seen by RFE/RL reveals growing concern about Russian aggression in the Baltic states, speaking of a "deteriorating security environment" amid an "increased frequency of airspace violations and drone incursions." The letter was sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and signed by the three Baltic European commissioners, Kaja Kallas, Andrius Kubilius, and Valdis Dombrovskis, as well as the Polish and Finnish commissioners. Dated July 30, the letter was one of a series of alarm bells sounded about Russian aggression over the course of the summer that culminated in CIA Director John Ratcliffe's surprise visit to Moscow on August 25. Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to urge the Kremlin against escalating with US allies -- particularly Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania -- sources briefed about the visit confirmed to RFE/RL on August 26. 'Every Six Months' Axios quoted Trump as denying Ratcliffe had issued such a warning to the Russians. "Ratcliffe sees his Russian counterpart once every six months or once every year. They have a very good relationship. There was no message and there was nothing unusual," Trump said. But when asked about the matter later by reporters in the Oval Office, Trump appeared to back off, saying "I don't want to comment on that, but they're not going to attack [NATO]." The New York Times, citing current and former officials, said Ratcliffe gave his counterpart a bleak assessment of the state of the Russia's war against Ukraine and to urge the Kremlin to reach a deal before its military and economic situation becomes worse. The Wall Street Journal earlier cited US intelligence as stating Russia may test NATO resolve with a limited incursion as early as this fall. Baltic diplomats who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity confirmed there was additional intelligence during the summer of Russian false-flag operations but no indication about an imminent conventional attack. They were also keen to point out that such operations might not be limited to the Baltics, a concern reinforced by recent cases of alleged or suspected Russian involvement in assassination attempts, fires, and drone incursions in several NATO countries, including Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. NATO Members Pressed Separately, a senior Pentagon official on August 27 pressed NATO allies to outline how they were answering US demands that they take more responsibility for Europe's defense as Washington reviews its force levels on the continent. The US administration under Trump has ignited fears among allies that the US could cut back its forces in Europe following a six-month review that began in July. "The spirit that we come in is obviously one...of consultation, of engagement. We want to hear from our allies," US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said during a visit for talks at NATO's headquarters in Brussels. Washington has sent out a questionnaire asking European countries to explain their efforts in taking the forefront in protecting the continent. "We're actually having a kind of down-to-business conversation about how we go forward together in a world in which Europe, which is obviously a very wealthy continent, can and is taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defense," Colby said. By RFE/RL

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Darya Shipilova died on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in Shelekhov. Photograph: Social Media View image in fullscreen Darya Shipilova died on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in Shelekhov. Photograph: Social Media Russia Lab worker ‘possibly’ dies of plague in Siberia, prompting quarantine measures Precautions in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia amid uncertainty over death of Darya Shipilova Pjotr Sauer and Luke Harding Mon 5 Oct 2026 06.47 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Several hospitals in Siberia have been placed under quarantine after the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague institute. Darya Shipilova, an employee at an institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, died on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov two days after falling ill. It remains unclear how she became unwell. Unconfirmed reports circulating in Russian media have suggested Shipilova, who was in her late twenties, may have been infected at work after an accident at the laboratory. Officials have not publicly confirmed that account. The uncertainty has been compounded by conflicting messages from politicians. Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the Buryatia region, which neighbours Irkutsk, initially wrote that she had died of plague, before editing his post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology” . It insisted that tests found no micro-organisms linked to her professional work and described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the area as stable. Authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk briefly urged residents to avoid travelling to Shelekhov and surrounding settlements after what they described as unofficial information about a possible plague infection. They later deleted the post from social media. “There are no obvious changes to daily life on the streets, but people are worried and anxious. Locals are angry that they are not being told anything,” said Elena Trifonova, a journalist with People of Baikal , an exiled Russian media outlet specialising on Siberia. Despite the lack of a confirmed diagnosis, a series of precautionary measures appear to have been introduced across the region. The US-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on Monday that several hospitals in Irkutsk had been placed under quarantine. The outlet said staff at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East had reportedly been isolated inside the institute since 2 October. Patients at Irkutsk city clinical hospital No 1 and the Ivano-Matreninskaya children’s hospital said relatives were not being allowed to visit and people inside were not permitted to leave. Only the delivery of food and personal items is allowed. Local media also reported quarantine measures at hospitals No 3 and No 10 and at least one maternity hospital. The restrictions have reportedly been imposed for three weeks. Elsewhere in the region, a mask requirement was introduced at the Irkutsk aluminium smelter in Shelekhov. The plant’s director, Artyom Fominykh, called it a preventive measure , saying: “Better safe than sorry.” Over the weekend several public events in Irkutsk were cancelled. The incident also prompted intervention from senior federal health officials. Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and the country’s chief sanitary doctor, travelled to Irkutsk last Friday. She attended an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission convened over what officials called a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection”. Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, urged residents to remain calm after meeting Popova to coordinate the response. “All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none is showing signs of illness and laboratory tests have returned negative results,” he wrote on Telegram. Kobzev made no reference to reports that a laboratory worker had died. Several US representatives have called for sweeping bans on flights from Russia. “We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk oblast, Russia,” the US Department of State told Radio Free Europe , adding that it was closely monitoring the situation together with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the US health agency. It urged the Russian authorities to “share accurate information quickly and openly”, while noting that plague was treatable with commonly available antibiotics, particularly when treatment began early. Plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian far east, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents and their fleas. But human cases in Russia are rare. Before the suspected Irkutsk case, the country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in Siberia’s Altai Republic contracted plague after helping butcher a marmot. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4.text: Image source, Reuters By Nick Thorpe ,Â Correspondent, Tirana, Albania Â and Â Toby Mann Published 8 hours ago Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes. The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence. "The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen". A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation. The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack." In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait. Image caption, People in Rinia park loosen cobblestones to use as ammunition against riot police A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters. Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas. Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range. "The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested. "In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop â completely unrelated to the protests, he said. "Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said. Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem. Image caption, Protesters were ready with saline spray to help to relieve the effects of tear gas Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her. "In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK." The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said. She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it. "When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said. "They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up." At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down. "We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups. Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said. "I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said. Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.
